full_text:
Interviewer:	You’re doing the design and technology course, aren’t you?

Subject:	Yep.

Interviewer:	I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing to begin with. The research that we’re looking at is mainly looking at engineering students. We’ve included the design and technology students because we’re also doing the study at [name] university and the design and technology side falls under engineering there, and generally because the project is looking at the male dominated industry, and I think that design technology is quite male dominated too. So we’re looking at people that are going on work placements mainly, are you going on a placement (yes) to see what their expectations of the placement are, then we’re going back to them when they’re on placement as well, and we’re also getting a few ideas about their experiences of education so far. So I’ll start off asking you a few background questions about why you decided to design and technology and that sort of thing, ok? What ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	I did biology, PE, English and design.

Interviewer:	What type of school did you go to?

Subject:	A really rubbish one (laughs) just one in a little town outside [town] in [area] a little, not that many people in it, and it had a sixth form in it.

Interviewer:	Was it mixed?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Er, all my work experience wasn’t really design.

Interviewer:	What do your parents do, are either of them designers?

Subject:	My dad’s like a engineer for [company] and my Mum is like a shop assistant, works in a chemist.

Interviewer:	So when and why do you think you decided to design and technology?

Subject:	Well, I wasn’t even going to pick it as an ‘A’ level, because we were the first ones to go through the new ‘AS’ levels, so we had to pick 4 instead of 3, so I had to pick a 4th one, so I picked design ‘cos I liked drawing and stuff and I liked doing design, and I’ve got a an A at GSCE, so I thought I’d do that one as an extra one, and I can drop it after a year, but I ended up dropping biology instead, ‘cos I really like design. And then erm, I was looking for a universities that was something I could do, and I was thinking about doing sports science, but then I didn’t realise that you could do design tech, ‘cos we hadn’t been told anything, and I looked it up and found that you could and I don’t live far from here, and I come here a lot ‘cos I used to do running, so I used the track a lot, and this was, I think, one of the best unis for doing industrial design so I decided to do that instead because I thought it was what I enjoyed more than, ‘cos I enjoy it more than doing like sciencey things.

Interviewer:	Did you have much careers guidance or anything?

Subject:	No, nothing really at school.

Interviewer:	How did you find out about the subject? When you started looking through university prospectuses?

Subject:	Yes and books and things.

Interviewer:	What about your family, have they been supportive?

Subject:	Yeah, my Dad’s really into it because he likes all drawing and making things and stuff, with him being an engineer as well, he always helps me do it. 

Interviewer:	Did you always know that you wanted to do the sandwich course?

Subject:	I thought it would help me a lot more in getting a job, so that’s why I wanted to do it and I thought its only an extra year, so.

Interviewer:	When you first started to do design and technology, did you realise that it was quite so male dominated?

Subject:	No, I didn’t realise at all. Like in my school I was the only one that did it out of the girls, but I didn’t think it’d be like that at uni, I thought there might be quite a lot of girls, but I think its because here it’s a lot like mechanics and electronics based, so I think that’s a lot more why, because girls tend to just steer away from that I think.

Interviewer:	Did it bother you at all when you realised it was so male-dominated?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to do design technology?

Subject:	Yeah because then I’d have more friends (laughs), all my friends are boys, so yeah, there’s not many girls on my course.

Interviewer:	What do you think could be done to encourage more women into it?

Subject:	I think they need to tell you more what it’s about, like its not just the insides of products and everything, its all drawing, its making it look good, and I think girls could be a lot better at that than men, so I think they need to be told about it more.

Interviewer:	What characteristics then do you think make a good designer?

Subject:	Erm, I think you’ve got to know what looks good, you’ve got to like be able to look into like future trends and design products from what you think its going to be like in the future, not what you think is now, ‘cos when you’re design something its not going to be made for like another 3 or 4 years, so you’ve got to be able to know what looks good. I don’t know, this is really hard.

Interviewer:	You said earlier that if there was more information, more girls might do it, so do you think that there’s anything that girls are better than boys at, or boys are better than girls?

Subject:	I think the girls are better at the colour side of things, choosing colour and I think the lads are better at seeing what the product could do and the insides of it, making it more like (?) and knowing all the stuff about that so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman in a male-dominated environment?

Subject:	Erm, you get more help, but I don’t know if you’re supposed to. I don’t know, people offer to help me a lot more, but I don’t usually take them up on it because I like to do it myself.

Interviewer:	Do you find that patronising at all?

Subject:	Yes, a lot, because at the moment we’re making like electronic products, we’re just making the outside of it, models in the workshop, and they’re all like ooh girls in the workshop, do you want me to help you, do you think sand that piece alright? Yeah I’m fine thanks. And people try to help you more, but I’d just rather do it myself.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

Subject:	Erm, I think boys are probably, I think men are probably took more seriously than women in it. I don’t think, erm, I think more men have got design jobs than women have, but I don’t know whether that’s just to do with the numbers, but I think they’re took a bit more seriously probably. 

Interviewer:	Has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Its been a lot harder. Its been a lot more hours than I thought it’d be, its like 24-7, just working. Like I’ve got lectures most of the day, and then I’m working at night to do the stuff that they’ve set us in our lectures, its just non-stop, and it’s a bit more electronics based than I thought it would be, but apart from that there’s not much else really.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the best and the worse things about the course so far?

Subject:	I think the best is – the worse is the amount of work it is, but then that, I think that is good in another way because that’s what its like in industry, and if we don’t do it like that, then we’ll are go into industry and not be prepared for it. So, I think that’s good in a way. What’ve I just said, good or bad?

Interviewer:	Well it started as a bad thing, then went to a good thing.

Subject:	Good things are its very interactive. We don’t usually have just lectures in a lecture room, there’s usually about 20 of us and we’re all talking and that, so you get a lot more friends from it, and it’s a lot more like interactive, you get a lot more out of it. And, I like that at the end of it we’ve got something to show for it, we don’t just have an essay, we’ve got like a portfolio of work, and then products or whatever, so we’ve got something to show for what we’ve been doing.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you have to do quite a lot of group work?

Subject:	Yes, quite a lot, yeah. And even if we’re doing individual projects its usually like, we get in a group first to talk about it, because you need others feedback otherwise you can’t – if you’re stuck for ideas, its good to talk to other people.

Interviewer:	When you do group work, how do you decide who you work with?

Subject:	Its, they usually put us in groups, if not then they say like a group of 4 or whatever, and I go with my friends, but not friends who are not very good at it. I usually go with people who work quite hard.

Interviewer:	Do you find that men or women are better to work with?

Subject:	Erm, I usually work with like one girl and mostly other boys. I think the lads work quite hard.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Yeah. I think they bring different ideas to it, things that they wouldn’t have thought about, we do and the other way around.

Interviewer:	Have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Errm, I had a bit of a bad one last semester. We were doing a, like a really big project in a group, and er, it was me and another girl and two boys and they were doing the workshop work and told us to do the presentation board, so we went away to do them and we got them finished like the day before we had to have them printed, so we gave them to the lads to look at and they changed it all over night, and gave it back to me, and went you can go and print it now, and I went to print it and it was completely different to what we’d done, and we’d spent like three days doing it. So that was a bit annoying, they obviously thought that it wasn’t good enough but they’d changed it to a really blokey thing, and it wasn’t – like his was all really dark colours and really harsh text and stuff, and it was supposed to be a kid’s product, so we didn’t really like it that much, but.

Interviewer:	Do you think they would’ve done that…

Subject:	To another boy? No, I think he thought we were a bit of a walk-over.

Interviewer:	What did you do about it then?

Subject:	Nothing, I just printed it off, I couldn’t be bothered to argue with him.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you had any female lecturers?

Subject:	Er yeah we did. We had a really good one, but she’s left at Christmas. She was brilliant, she was a lot better than anyone else I’d say. She was very like, very enthusiastic about everything.

Interviewer:	Do you think that was to do with her being a woman or?

Subject:	Yes, I think a lot of it was, she was trying to get back at, it was all men in the department and now her, and now its all men now.

Interviewer:	Would you like to see more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, everyone was really good when she took us, even the lads, she was just really motivating about everything, and really like inspirational.

Interviewer:	Do the male lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

Subject:	No, erm, not like really badly. Some are fine, but there’s some that always try and help you if you’re a girl which is a bit annoying.

Interviewer:	Have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male as well?

Subject:	Yes, he’s actually not a very nice man. 

Interviewer:	Is that just him or would you rather have a female personal tutor?

Subject:	I, erm, I don’t mind it being a man, but he’s just not a very nice one, he’s a bit weird.

Interviewer:	Not approachable then?

Subject:	No, no I wouldn’t ever approach him for anything. There’s a few of them who are really nice, who I’d go to before I go to him about anything.

Interviewer:	Is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	What lecturers?

Interviewer:	Or friends, or something that’s happened?

Subject:	I live in a house with, all designers, and one of them is really erm hard-working and everything, and I think he’s helped us all do a lot more, because he’ll say look we shouldn’t be sitting watching tele, we should be doing work, and then we’ll all go and do it, rather, or if we’re sitting doing nothing and he’s doing it, it makes you feel bad, so you go and do it, so I think he’s helped us all a lot. 

Interviewer:	Ok, is there any part of the teaching or advice that you’ve had that you think will help you on your placement?

Subject:	We haven’t really had much help with our placement at all. It was just erm, ‘cos most people haven’t really applied yet. I just got mine quite early. But we haven’t really had much advice on it. We had a talk from the careers service lady on campus, but that was about it really, we haven’t had any help really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll take a lot of the skills from the course onto the placement?

Subject:	Erm, not as many as I would, ‘cos mines a research and development placement, rather than like pure design, so I don’t think, so there won’t be as much sketching and design, more like the research side of our course. But I think a lot of the stuff I’ve done, because we’ve been doing quite a few research projects at the moment, so I think they’ll help. 

Interviewer:	What about interpersonal skills and things like that?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah I think its helped because we have to do like presentations standing up in front of everyone and stuff, I think all that’ll help, that I’ve done that before I go, ‘cos for my interview I had to do like a 10 minute presentation, like I’d never have done that like a year ago, but ‘cos we have to do it quite a lot, it just makes you a bit more at ease with it. I mean its never easy but its, I’ve got a lot better at it now.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there’s anything that you’ve learnt from previous work experience that will help you on your placement?

Subject:	Erm, not really, my work experience wasn’t very good. I worked in a hospital, erm. I don’t know, I think I can get along with people a lot better now. I’m a lot more confident when I’m talking to people, ‘cos I was really shy when I first, on like my first ever placement. But now I’ve got a job as well, I work at the cinema in town, and that helps, ‘cos like I’m serving people and dealing with customers and stuff, it just gets you a lot more used to it, so I think I’ll be a lot better at talking to people and communicating.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like ready to go on placement?

Subject:	No, not at all, I’m really scared.

Interviewer:	What bits are you scared about?

Subject:	Er, I’m scared that I won’t be able to do what they ask me to do, but I, erm, the girl who’s there at the moment on the placement, like she sat with us while our interviews were going on, so like in between our interviews she sat with us, and I was talking to her quite a lot, and she was like, oh, you’ll be able to do it, so, it wasn’t as bad, but its still a bit scary going into like a company like Mars and just.

Interviewer:	Do you think there should be more information about what to expect, would that help you?

Subject:	Yeah, I think they should send out like. Well, I think uni should help you a lot more’cos we’ve had nothing really, we don’t know what its going to be like at all. Most people haven’t even sent anything off, they don’t know what they’re doing next year, whether they’re coming back or going on placement, ‘cos we don’t get much help with it, but.

Interviewer:	What do you think the university could do to help?

Subject:	I think they need more like afternoons where they just have stuff for placements and people, like more companies coming in and telling us that they’ve got placements ‘cos we don’t know where to look and stuff. I think they need to have a lot more communication with companies and then get in contact with us to tell us about it. ‘Cos we just get emails from the bloke who sorts its out saying, oh there might be a placement here or whatever, but you have to do it all yourself and it’s a bit, gone from nothing to everything really, it’s a bit hard.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that the whole educational experience and the way your taught reflects what its going to be like in the industry? You said like, the hours you think will help?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	How do you think work will differ from being at uni?

Subject:	I think I’ll be a bit more of a skivvy probably. I don’t think it is going to be as taxing as this, because like, I’m used to working from 9 til like 9 at night, so I don’t think its going to be as hard. I think its just going to be more, its just going to be different I think, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Ok, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, I wasn’t gonna go, but I decided to go and then last year when I was in my first year, I thought oh I dunno if I want to go anymore, because our course is so competitive and I just thought I’m not gonna get on, as they’re all so competitive, and they kept saying there’s only like 20 out of a 100 people that usually get placements and things, and I just thought, oh I don’t know if I even want to bother, but my mum and dad were just like do what you want to do, or they kept saying that I could just come home for a year and just get a job if I wanted a rest from the course as it is really, but they were just saying do what you wanna do really. My boyfriend wanted me to do it, but that’s ‘cos he failed his first year, and wanted me here for his last year.
Interviewer:	What do you think are the advantages of doing a placement then?

Subject:	I think it will just help you get a job more and it will help, I’ll know what its like to be in a full-time job and what sort of work places do and things. I think it’ll help – look good on my CV.

Interviewer:	Did you say its [company] that you’re going to work for?

Subject:	Yes, its [company] in [town].

Interviewer:	How did you decide to go and work for them? What attracted you to that company?

Subject:	Well its close to here, which is like close to home and uni, because most of my friends are in their last year next year so I want to be here so I can still be with them if you know what I mean. So I can travel to it, and its close to my home, so I can travel home easily, and erm its not far from here, so I can be back by like half five. And erm, they’re a big company, so I thought was good ‘cos they really like, important company and they sent a letter to uni saying that they had some vacancies and you had to fill in an online application form, so I did that and then got an interview, so.

Interviewer:	Did you apply to anywhere else?

Subject:	No that was the only one. It’s the best paid one out of all the placements as well, so I was like yes I’ll take that.

Interviewer:	Did you look at things like training opportunities or like career prospects or anything like that?

Subject:	Erm, within the role? Erm I think they do a postgraduate thing, but doing the placement year doesn’t help you at all to get on to the programme, which I think is rubbish (laughing). They should help you if you’ve been with them for a year, but erm I think they do all your training while you’re there. They’ve haven’t told me much about it really.

Interviewer:	Do you know what sort of work you’ll be doing when you get there?

Subject:	No they just said research and development and they’d send me some more information, so I don’t know. My tutor told me that I’ll be analysing [product], [product]. I’m like oh great.

Interviewer:	Did you do much research into the company?

Subject:	I just looked on their website to see what it was like before my interview and stuff. They’re a bit American, its all like the principles of [company] and stuff like that. I just looked at that, so I didn’t go thinking it was something that it wasn’t.

Interviewer:	Did you have the opportunity at all to be sponsored?

Subject:	Er, no. I think we’ve got to be sponsored for our final year project.

Interviewer:	What sort of things are you hoping to get out of the placement?

Subject:	Erm, money? Er, Just some experience, because I think that’s what I’d rather do, something like, but I don’t think I want to do the full on design, doing the design consultancy thing, I think I’d rather do the research, or like the marketing side of it, so I’m quite happy that I got this one ‘cos its not just all designing, so I think it’ll give me a lot of experience, and I’ll see if that is what I really want to do. 

Interviewer:	Do you think you’ll have much opportunity to put into practice everything you’ve learnt?

Subject:	I hope so, I hope they’re not just going to (use?) me.

Interviewer:	Ok, what do you think will be the best and worst things about going on placement?

Subject:	Erm, the best would be the money, cos I’ve got none and I really need to pay off my overdraft, and that I can still stay in [university town]. Worst – at first its going to be horrible meeting everyone, and not knowing anyone. Travelling’s not going to be nice, ‘cos its ¾ of an hour everyday there and back. But I think I’ll enjoy the placement, and just doing the job will be quite fun – its just something different, isn’t it?

Interviewer:	In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say five years time?

Subject:	Erm, travelling. I want to travel after uni for a few years. I don’t want to get a job! After uni, I want a break. I think I’ll get a job for a bit to get some money, and then I wanna go travelling, and then I want like, I’d like to do a marketing job after that and be the head of a big marketing firm, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Is that your ideal career then?

Subject:	I don’t think I could go that far up, I don’t think I can tell people what to do very well, but no I’m not that strong-willed I don’t think.

Interviewer:	Ok, what sort of things do you think will get in the way of you achieving that?

Subject:	Erm, when I go travelling and I don’t want to come back. 

Interviewer:	Would you like a job that involves travelling then?

Subject:	Erm, yes I would, erm I don’t know, yeah I think I would yeah. I don’t want to stay in  England, it bores me staying in one place for too long – I’m really bored of [university town] already.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the career prospects are good in the design and technology industry?

Subject:	No, there’s not many jobs I don’t think, and they’re really like competitive and really short-lived if you do get one I think ‘cos they’re that competitive, they’re just looking for new people all the time, who can do better so, I think it’ll be quite hard to get a job, but I want to go more down the marketing route I think, so I don’t think – its not as worrying.

Interviewer:	Ok, are you happy with all the career choice s that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	No, I only think I would because I wanted to do athletics so much when I came here. I can’t do it anymore because my course, its too much work, and I’d have to not do my work as well, and that’s what I’ve come here for really, so I’ve had to give up that. But I always think I should’ve done a degree that’s 6 hours a week so I could carry on running, but I wouldn’t.

Interviewer:	Was that quite a surprise to you then, coming to [this university]?

Subject:	Yes, ‘cos I thought that I’d be able to do it because its very into sport as well, and I know loads of people here who do running and I see them everyday running round, and I’m not doing it anymore, but it wasn’t so bad ‘cos all my friends do 8 hours a week or whatever, and I have like 20 and loads of work on top of that, so it’s a bit annoying but I think the course had to come first because that’s what I’m going to do in the long run, I’m not going to run in the Olympics or anything like that so, I’ve got to put my course first.

Interviewer:	Do you find it strange that you’re based in the social sciences faculty and not the engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, I thought that was a bit weird, why is that? Last year we had like 30 hours, and now its about 20.

Interviewer:	Here’s a tricky one for you now. What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the industry?

Subject:	God, you should have sent me these questions before! Erm, competitive, hard-working, erm, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it is masculine?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Why?

Subject:	Its just so male-dominated. And like a lot of the projects we do its all like car design and all this, and its just like that’s all they talk about, and ‘cos we’ve just got male lecturers they don’t even know that they’re doing it, yet all they’re talking about is, if you look on this car design website or of you look on (lost words?), its all male.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’ll stay like that, or do you think…

Subject:	Yeah, until you get a lady like that one who left come back and try and shake it up a bit.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that any aspects of the culture and the fact that its so male-dominated will cause any problems for you trying to get a job or anything like that?

Subject:	Erm, I think it’ll be harder in the pure design ones like in a consultancy, ‘cos I think they won’t take you as seriously, but I don’t think it will in other areas, like what I’m going for my placement in. I think its more like in a consultancy where they’re all sat down designed around the table – I think they’d rather have a man there than a woman.

Interviewer:	Ok, that’s everything, thank you.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I didn’t realise at all. Like in my school I was the only one that did it out of the girls, but I didn’t think it’d be like that at uni, I thought there might be quite a lot of girls, but I think its because here it’s a lot like mechanics and electronics based, so I think that’s a lot more why, because girls tend to just steer away from that I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it bother you at all when you realised it was so male-dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to do design technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah because then I’d have more friends (laughs), all my friends are boys, so yeah, there’s not many girls on my course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think could be done to encourage more women into it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they need to tell you more what it’s about, like its not just the insides of products and everything, its all drawing, its making it look good, and I think girls could be a lot better at that than men, so I think they need to be told about it more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What characteristics then do you think make a good designer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think you’ve got to know what looks good, you’ve got to like be able to look into like future trends and design products from what you think its going to be like in the future, not what you think is now, ‘cos when you’re design something its not going to be made for like another 3 or 4 years, so you’ve got to be able to know what looks good. I don’t know, this is really hard.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said earlier that if there was more information, more girls might do it, so do you think that there’s anything that girls are better than boys at, or boys are better than girls?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the girls are better at the colour side of things, choosing colour and I think the lads are better at seeing what the product could do and the insides of it, making it more like (?) and knowing all the stuff about that so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman in a male-dominated environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, you get more help, but I don’t know if you’re supposed to. I don’t know, people offer to help me a lot more, but I don’t usually take them up on it because I like to do it myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find that patronising at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, a lot, because at the moment we’re making like electronic products, we’re just making the outside of it, models in the workshop, and they’re all like ooh girls in the workshop, do you want me to help you, do you think sand that piece alright? Yeah I’m fine thanks. And people try to help you more, but I’d just rather do it myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think boys are probably, I think men are probably took more seriously than women in it. I don’t think, erm, I think more men have got design jobs than women have, but I don’t know whether that’s just to do with the numbers, but I think they’re took a bit more seriously probably.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Its been a lot harder. Its been a lot more hours than I thought it’d be, its like 24-7, just working. Like I’ve got lectures most of the day, and then I’m working at night to do the stuff that they’ve set us in our lectures, its just non-stop, and it’s a bit more electronics based than I thought it would be, but apart from that there’s not much else really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the best and the worse things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the best is – the worse is the amount of work it is, but then that, I think that is good in another way because that’s what its like in industry, and if we don’t do it like that, then we’ll are go into industry and not be prepared for it. So, I think that’s good in a way. What’ve I just said, good or bad?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well it started as a bad thing, then went to a good thing.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Good things are its very interactive. We don’t usually have just lectures in a lecture room, there’s usually about 20 of us and we’re all talking and that, so you get a lot more friends from it, and it’s a lot more like interactive, you get a lot more out of it. And, I like that at the end of it we’ve got something to show for it, we don’t just have an essay, we’ve got like a portfolio of work, and then products or whatever, so we’ve got something to show for what we’ve been doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you have to do quite a lot of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, quite a lot, yeah. And even if we’re doing individual projects its usually like, we get in a group first to talk about it, because you need others feedback otherwise you can’t – if you’re stuck for ideas, its good to talk to other people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you do group work, how do you decide who you work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Its, they usually put us in groups, if not then they say like a group of 4 or whatever, and I go with my friends, but not friends who are not very good at it. I usually go with people who work quite hard.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find that men or women are better to work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I usually work with like one girl and mostly other boys. I think the lads work quite hard.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I think they bring different ideas to it, things that they wouldn’t have thought about, we do and the other way around.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Errm, I had a bit of a bad one last semester. We were doing a, like a really big project in a group, and er, it was me and another girl and two boys and they were doing the workshop work and told us to do the presentation board, so we went away to do them and we got them finished like the day before we had to have them printed, so we gave them to the lads to look at and they changed it all over night, and gave it back to me, and went you can go and print it now, and I went to print it and it was completely different to what we’d done, and we’d spent like three days doing it. So that was a bit annoying, they obviously thought that it wasn’t good enough but they’d changed it to a really blokey thing, and it wasn’t – like his was all really dark colours and really harsh text and stuff, and it was supposed to be a kid’s product, so we didn’t really like it that much, but.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think they would’ve done that…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To another boy? No, I think he thought we were a bit of a walk-over.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What did you do about it then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Nothing, I just printed it off, I couldn’t be bothered to argue with him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you had any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er yeah we did. We had a really good one, but she’s left at Christmas. She was brilliant, she was a lot better than anyone else I’d say. She was very like, very enthusiastic about everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that was to do with her being a woman or?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think a lot of it was, she was trying to get back at, it was all men in the department and now her, and now its all men now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like to see more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, everyone was really good when she took us, even the lads, she was just really motivating about everything, and really like inspirational.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do the male lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, erm, not like really badly. Some are fine, but there’s some that always try and help you if you’re a girl which is a bit annoying.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, he’s actually not a very nice man.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that just him or would you rather have a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I, erm, I don’t mind it being a man, but he’s just not a very nice one, he’s a bit weird.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not approachable then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, no I wouldn’t ever approach him for anything. There’s a few of them who are really nice, who I’d go to before I go to him about anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What lecturers?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Or friends, or something that’s happened?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I live in a house with, all designers, and one of them is really erm hard-working and everything, and I think he’s helped us all do a lot more, because he’ll say look we shouldn’t be sitting watching tele, we should be doing work, and then we’ll all go and do it, rather, or if we’re sitting doing nothing and he’s doing it, it makes you feel bad, so you go and do it, so I think he’s helped us all a lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, is there any part of the teaching or advice that you’ve had that you think will help you on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We haven’t really had much help with our placement at all. It was just erm, ‘cos most people haven’t really applied yet. I just got mine quite early. But we haven’t really had much advice on it. We had a talk from the careers service lady on campus, but that was about it really, we haven’t had any help really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll take a lot of the skills from the course onto the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not as many as I would, ‘cos mines a research and development placement, rather than like pure design, so I don’t think, so there won’t be as much sketching and design, more like the research side of our course. But I think a lot of the stuff I’ve done, because we’ve been doing quite a few research projects at the moment, so I think they’ll help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about interpersonal skills and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah I think its helped because we have to do like presentations standing up in front of everyone and stuff, I think all that’ll help, that I’ve done that before I go, ‘cos for my interview I had to do like a 10 minute presentation, like I’d never have done that like a year ago, but ‘cos we have to do it quite a lot, it just makes you a bit more at ease with it. I mean its never easy but its, I’ve got a lot better at it now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there’s anything that you’ve learnt from previous work experience that will help you on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really, my work experience wasn’t very good. I worked in a hospital, erm. I don’t know, I think I can get along with people a lot better now. I’m a lot more confident when I’m talking to people, ‘cos I was really shy when I first, on like my first ever placement. But now I’ve got a job as well, I work at the cinema in town, and that helps, ‘cos like I’m serving people and dealing with customers and stuff, it just gets you a lot more used to it, so I think I’ll be a lot better at talking to people and communicating.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like ready to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not at all, I’m really scared.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What bits are you scared about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I’m scared that I won’t be able to do what they ask me to do, but I, erm, the girl who’s there at the moment on the placement, like she sat with us while our interviews were going on, so like in between our interviews she sat with us, and I was talking to her quite a lot, and she was like, oh, you’ll be able to do it, so, it wasn’t as bad, but its still a bit scary going into like a company like Mars and just.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there should be more information about what to expect, would that help you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think they should send out like. Well, I think uni should help you a lot more’cos we’ve had nothing really, we don’t know what its going to be like at all. Most people haven’t even sent anything off, they don’t know what they’re doing next year, whether they’re coming back or going on placement, ‘cos we don’t get much help with it, but.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think the university could do to help?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they need more like afternoons where they just have stuff for placements and people, like more companies coming in and telling us that they’ve got placements ‘cos we don’t know where to look and stuff. I think they need to have a lot more communication with companies and then get in contact with us to tell us about it. ‘Cos we just get emails from the bloke who sorts its out saying, oh there might be a placement here or whatever, but you have to do it all yourself and it’s a bit, gone from nothing to everything really, it’s a bit hard.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that the whole educational experience and the way your taught reflects what its going to be like in the industry? You said like, the hours you think will help?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think work will differ from being at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I’ll be a bit more of a skivvy probably. I don’t think it is going to be as taxing as this, because like, I’m used to working from 9 til like 9 at night, so I don’t think its going to be as hard. I think its just going to be more, its just going to be different I think, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I wasn’t gonna go, but I decided to go and then last year when I was in my first year, I thought oh I dunno if I want to go anymore, because our course is so competitive and I just thought I’m not gonna get on, as they’re all so competitive, and they kept saying there’s only like 20 out of a 100 people that usually get placements and things, and I just thought, oh I don’t know if I even want to bother, but my mum and dad were just like do what you want to do, or they kept saying that I could just come home for a year and just get a job if I wanted a rest from the course as it is really, but they were just saying do what you wanna do really. My boyfriend wanted me to do it, but that’s ‘cos he failed his first year, and wanted me here for his last year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the advantages of doing a placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will just help you get a job more and it will help, I’ll know what its like to be in a full-time job and what sort of work places do and things. I think it’ll help – look good on my CV.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you say its [company] that you’re going to work for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, its [company] in [town].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide to go and work for them? What attracted you to that company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well its close to here, which is like close to home and uni, because most of my friends are in their last year next year so I want to be here so I can still be with them if you know what I mean. So I can travel to it, and its close to my home, so I can travel home easily, and erm its not far from here, so I can be back by like half five. And erm, they’re a big company, so I thought was good ‘cos they really like, important company and they sent a letter to uni saying that they had some vacancies and you had to fill in an online application form, so I did that and then got an interview, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you apply to anywhere else?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No that was the only one. It’s the best paid one out of all the placements as well, so I was like yes I’ll take that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you look at things like training opportunities or like career prospects or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, within the role? Erm I think they do a postgraduate thing, but doing the placement year doesn’t help you at all to get on to the programme, which I think is rubbish (laughing). They should help you if you’ve been with them for a year, but erm I think they do all your training while you’re there. They’ve haven’t told me much about it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know what sort of work you’ll be doing when you get there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No they just said research and development and they’d send me some more information, so I don’t know. My tutor told me that I’ll be analysing [product], [product]. I’m like oh great.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do much research into the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I just looked on their website to see what it was like before my interview and stuff. They’re a bit American, its all like the principles of [company] and stuff like that. I just looked at that, so I didn’t go thinking it was something that it wasn’t.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have the opportunity at all to be sponsored?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, no. I think we’ve got to be sponsored for our final year project.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of things are you hoping to get out of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, money? Er, Just some experience, because I think that’s what I’d rather do, something like, but I don’t think I want to do the full on design, doing the design consultancy thing, I think I’d rather do the research, or like the marketing side of it, so I’m quite happy that I got this one ‘cos its not just all designing, so I think it’ll give me a lot of experience, and I’ll see if that is what I really want to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you’ll have much opportunity to put into practice everything you’ve learnt?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so, I hope they’re not just going to (use?) me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what do you think will be the best and worst things about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the best would be the money, cos I’ve got none and I really need to pay off my overdraft, and that I can still stay in [university town]. Worst – at first its going to be horrible meeting everyone, and not knowing anyone. Travelling’s not going to be nice, ‘cos its ¾ of an hour everyday there and back. But I think I’ll enjoy the placement, and just doing the job will be quite fun – its just something different, isn’t it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in say five years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, travelling. I want to travel after uni for a few years. I don’t want to get a job! After uni, I want a break. I think I’ll get a job for a bit to get some money, and then I wanna go travelling, and then I want like, I’d like to do a marketing job after that and be the head of a big marketing firm, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think I could go that far up, I don’t think I can tell people what to do very well, but no I’m not that strong-willed I don’t think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what sort of things do you think will get in the way of you achieving that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, when I go travelling and I don’t want to come back.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like a job that involves travelling then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yes I would, erm I don’t know, yeah I think I would yeah. I don’t want to stay in England, it bores me staying in one place for too long – I’m really bored of [university town] already.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the career prospects are good in the design and technology industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, there’s not many jobs I don’t think, and they’re really like competitive and really short-lived if you do get one I think ‘cos they’re that competitive, they’re just looking for new people all the time, who can do better so, I think it’ll be quite hard to get a job, but I want to go more down the marketing route I think, so I don’t think – its not as worrying.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, are you happy with all the career choice s that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I only think I would because I wanted to do athletics so much when I came here. I can’t do it anymore because my course, its too much work, and I’d have to not do my work as well, and that’s what I’ve come here for really, so I’ve had to give up that. But I always think I should’ve done a degree that’s 6 hours a week so I could carry on running, but I wouldn’t.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was that quite a surprise to you then, coming to [this university]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, ‘cos I thought that I’d be able to do it because its very into sport as well, and I know loads of people here who do running and I see them everyday running round, and I’m not doing it anymore, but it wasn’t so bad ‘cos all my friends do 8 hours a week or whatever, and I have like 20 and loads of work on top of that, so it’s a bit annoying but I think the course had to come first because that’s what I’m going to do in the long run, I’m not going to run in the Olympics or anything like that so, I’ve got to put my course first.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find it strange that you’re based in the social sciences faculty and not the engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I thought that was a bit weird, why is that? Last year we had like 30 hours, and now its about 20.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Here’s a tricky one for you now. What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: God, you should have sent me these questions before! Erm, competitive, hard-working, erm, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it is masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Its just so male-dominated. And like a lot of the projects we do its all like car design and all this, and its just like that’s all they talk about, and ‘cos we’ve just got male lecturers they don’t even know that they’re doing it, yet all they’re talking about is, if you look on this car design website or of you look on (lost words?), its all male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’ll stay like that, or do you think…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, until you get a lady like that one who left come back and try and shake it up a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that any aspects of the culture and the fact that its so male-dominated will cause any problems for you trying to get a job or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think it’ll be harder in the pure design ones like in a consultancy, ‘cos I think they won’t take you as seriously, but I don’t think it will in other areas, like what I’m going for my placement in. I think its more like in a consultancy where they’re all sat down designed around the table – I think they’d rather have a man there than a woman.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, that’s everything, thank you.
